Regard a blocked configuration as a maximal family of pairwise disjoint horizontal or vertical triples.

For the lower bound, suppose first that $n\ge 3$. There are $n(n-2)$ horizontal and $n(n-2)$ vertical potential triples, for a total of

$T=2n(n-2)$.

Every potential triple must meet a removed block; otherwise it could still be removed. A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal potential triples, since their starting positions lie in an interval of five positions. Each of its three cells lies in at most three vertical potential triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus any removed block meets at most $14$ potential triples; the vertical case is symmetric. Consequently, if $m$ blocks form a blocked configuration, then

$14m\ge 2n(n-2)$,

and hence

$m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n$.

This applies in particular to $b(n)$. For $n=1,2$, we have $b(n)=0$, and the same inequality remains valid. Thus we may take $c=2/7$.

For the upper bound, first construct a periodic packing on the infinite square grid. In every row $r\in\mathbb Z$, and for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, choose the horizontal block

$B_{r,k}=\{(r,r+5k),(r,r+5k+1),(r,r+5k+2)\}$.

These blocks are pairwise disjoint. A cell $(r,s)$ is covered exactly when $s-r\pmod 5$ belongs to $\{0,1,2\}$. Therefore every horizontal triple meets a chosen block, because among three consecutive residues modulo $5$ not all can belong to $\{3,4\}$. For a vertical triple, the three relevant residues are $s-r,s-r-1,s-r-2$, which likewise cannot all belong to $\{3,4\}$. Hence every horizontal or vertical triple in the infinite grid meets this packing.

Now restrict to the square $Q=\{1,\ldots,n\}^2$, retaining only those blocks $B_{r,k}$ lying wholly in $Q$; call this family $\mathcal P_0$. In any row, the retained blocks have starting positions spaced by $5$, so there are at most $(n+2)/5$ of them. Hence

$|\mathcal P_0|\le \frac{n(n+2)}5$.

Let

$S=\{(r,s)\in Q:s\le2\text{ or }s\ge n-1\}$.

Thus $|S|\le4n$. Any triple in $Q$ disjoint from $\mathcal P_0$ must meet $S$: it meets some block of the infinite packing, and because that block was not retained, the block crosses the left or right boundary, so its intersection with $Q$ lies in $S$.

Starting with $\mathcal P_0$, greedily add disjoint triples until no further triple can be added. Every added triple was already disjoint from $\mathcal P_0$, and therefore contains a cell of $S$. Since the added triples are mutually disjoint, distinct added triples contain distinct cells of $S$. Thus at most $4n$ blocks are added. The resulting configuration is blocked and uses at most

$\frac{n(n+2)}5+4n=\frac15n^2+\frac{22}{5}n\le \frac15n^2+5n$

blocks. Therefore $d=5$ is valid. Combining the two bounds proves the theorem for every positive integer $n$.

Let a potential triple mean three consecutive cells in one row or one column. A terminal configuration must meet every potential triple with at least one removed cell.

For n≥3, there are
\[
2n(n-2)
\]
potential triples. A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal potential triples: their starting columns can differ from the block's starting column by at most 2. Each of its three cells belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples altogether. The same argument applies to a vertical block.

Consequently, every terminal collection of m removed blocks satisfies
\[
14m\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
and hence
\[
m\ge \frac{n(n-2)}7=\frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
Therefore
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For n=1,2 this inequality also holds because b(n)=0. Thus we may take c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first define a periodic collection of horizontal blocks on the infinite integer grid. For every row r and integer k, let
\[
P_{r,k}=\{(r,r+5k),(r,r+5k+1),(r,r+5k+2)\}.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint. Their removed cells in any row occupy three consecutive residue classes modulo 5, leaving only two consecutive unremoved cells, so every horizontal potential triple meets one of them.

They also meet every vertical potential triple. Indeed, (r,c) belongs to one of these blocks exactly when
\[
c-r\pmod 5\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
For three consecutive rows r,r+1,r+2, the three residues
\[
c-r,\quad c-r-1,\quad c-r-2
\]
are distinct, so they cannot all lie in the two-element complement \(\{3,4\}\). Hence every vertical triple also meets the periodic pattern.

Now restrict to the n×n board and initially remove every block P_{r,k} that is wholly contained in it. In each row there are at most n/5+1 such blocks, so the number initially removed is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]
Let E be the set of board cells belonging to a periodic block that crosses the left or right boundary and therefore was not removed. In each row at most one block crosses each boundary, contributing at most two board cells there. Hence
\[
|E|\le 4n.
\]
Every potential triple remaining after the initial removals meets E: the corresponding infinite-grid triple meets the periodic pattern, and any patterned cell not already removed must belong to a boundary-crossing block.

Continue removing arbitrary available triples until none remain. Removing cells cannot create a new triple, so every triple removed during this continuation was already present after the initial removals and therefore contains a cell of E. The additionally removed blocks are disjoint, so distinct additional blocks contain distinct cells of E. Thus at most 4n additional blocks are removed.

This produces a terminal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+4n=\frac15n^2+5n
\]
blocks. Therefore
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+5n.
\]
Taking c=2/7 and d=5 proves, for every positive integer n,
\[
\frac17n^2-cn\le b(n)\le \frac15n^2+dn.
\]

Number the rows and columns by \(1,\dots,n\). We may assume \(n\) is a positive integer.

For \(n\le 2\), no block exists, so \(b(n)=0\). Now suppose \(n\ge3\).

There are \(n(n-2)\) horizontal triples and \(n(n-2)\) vertical triples, hence \(2n(n-2)\) potential blocks. In any terminal configuration, every such triple must contain a removed stamp.

A removed horizontal block meets at most five horizontal triples: their left endpoints can lie at most two positions before through two positions after the block's left endpoint. Each of its three stamps belongs to at most three vertical triples, so the block meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus any removed block, horizontal or vertical, meets at most \(5+9=14\) potential triples. Consequently
\[
14b(n)\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
This inequality also holds for \(n=1,2\). Thus we may take \(c=2/7\).

For the upper bound, first consider the infinite integer grid. In every row \(r\), place the horizontal blocks
\[
B_{r,q}=\{(r,r+5q),(r,r+5q+1),(r,r+5q+2)\},\qquad q\in\mathbb Z.
\]
These blocks are pairwise disjoint. A cell \((r,s)\) is not covered precisely when
\[
s-r\equiv 3\text{ or }4\pmod 5.
\]
Thus no horizontal triple is uncovered. Nor can a vertical triple in rows \(r,r+1,r+2\) be uncovered: writing \(x=s-r\pmod5\), this would require simultaneously
\[
x\in\{3,4\},\qquad x\in\{4,0\},\qquad x\in\{0,1\},
\]
which is impossible.

On the finite \(n\times n\) sheet, initially tear out all blocks \(B_{r,q}\) that lie entirely within the sheet. In each row their starting columns are spaced five apart, so there are at most \(n/5+1\) of them. Hence the initial number of blocks is at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n.
\]

Let
\[
S=\{(r,s):s\le4\text{ or }s\ge n-3\},
\]
the union of the first and last four columns. We claim that every triple still available after the initial removals lies entirely in \(S\). Indeed, the corresponding triple in the infinite grid meets some \(B_{r,q}\). Because the triple remains available, that infinite-grid block was omitted from the finite construction and therefore crossed the left or right edge. Its cells lying on the sheet have column \(1,2,n-1\), or \(n\). A vertical triple containing such a cell lies in \(S\), while a horizontal triple containing it lies within the first or last four columns.

Now greedily tear out available blocks until none remains. Removing stamps cannot create a new available triple, so every additionally chosen block was already available after the initial removals and is therefore contained in \(S\). These added blocks are disjoint, and \(|S|\le8n\), so their number is at most \(8n/3\). We have consequently produced a terminal configuration using at most
\[
\frac15n^2+n+\frac83n
=\frac15n^2+\frac{11}{3}n
\]
blocks. Therefore
\[
b(n)\le \frac15n^2+\frac{11}{3}n.
\]
Taking \(c=2/7\) and \(d=11/3\) proves the result for every positive integer \(n\).

problem.theorem:
I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).
